title.narrative: 1.1 Support rule of law by well-functioning national and regional human rights systems

In 2024 - by end-reporting medio 2025 - DIHR has achieved at least 2 additional state actors catalysing human rights coordination, enhancing respect for human rights and / or engaging in regional and international human rights systems.

target.value: DIHR has established 2 additional MoUs with Governmental Human Rights Focal Points, National Human Rights Institutions or other actor in the National Human Rights Systems (such as line ministries; local authorities; parliaments) The chain(s) of changes recorded in year one is continued in year 2; at least one new chain of changes / outcomes is recorded regarding international networking amongst Governmental Human Rights Focal Points. DIHR and other actors have got access to new guidance on Governmental Human Rights Focal Points and/or key actors involved in implementing Human Rights in the national contexts.

actual.value: An MoU was signed with South African Human Rights Commission to collaborate on tech and ongoing engagements with the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights on integrating tech in their work. Discussions initiated with the Ugandan Human Rights Commission and the Malawi Human Rights Commission on the development of a partnership with DIHR. Technical input to two high-level events in Geneva aimed at giving effect to the recommendations of the OHCHR report 50/64 of May 2022 on NMIRFs. In March, DIHR took the initiative to establish the NHRI Digital Rights Alliance. The Alliance has grown to NHRIs from 24 countries, and at least 10 NHRIs have drafted a concrete action plan on integrating digital rights into to their work and mandate areas. DIHR research explored GHRFPs in the Research Handbook on Implementation of Human Rights in Practice entitled 'Implementers or facilitators of implementation? Governmental human rights focal points' Also published "National HR Actionplans"

target.value: Chains of changes are continued. At least two chains of change are recorded with 'major' significance by peer assessor per partner in relation to realisation of output 1; in addition, at least one chain of change is recorded with significance no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per partner in relation to realisation of output indicator 1.1; Governmental Human Rights Focal Points, National Human Rights Institutions or other actor in the National Human Rights System (such as line ministries; local authorities; parliaments) have fulfilled their mandated and context relevant tasks in 2 countries. Two state actors / NHRIs are engaged in ensuring human rights-based framework for digitalization (good e-governance)

actual.value: DIHR has influenced 4 additional state actors during the DED period based partly or fully on DED funding (state actors include additional Governmental Human Rights Focal Points, National Human Rights Institutions or other actors in the National Human Rights System, such as line ministries, local authorities and parliaments). This figure is in addition to the cooperation with a range of NHRIs that were already well-established before the present DED e.g. in Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Honduras and Palestine. The new and additional state actors counted in this indicator include: the Governmental Human Rights Focal Point in Tunisia (CNRDH), the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), Ministry of Labour and Social Protection in Kenya and the NHRI in Cote d'Ivoire.

target.value: Chains of outcomes are continued. At least two chains of change are recorded with significance valued no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per. Chains of outcomes show that DIHR and other actors are applying new guidance on Governmental Human Rights Focal Points and/or key actors involved in implementing Human Rights in the national contexts.

actual.value: Regarding additional state actors catalysing human rights coordination, DIHR has cooperated with 3 additional state actors based partly on DED funding, namely the NHRI in Cote d'Ivoire, the National Centre for Human Rights in Jordan and the Ministry of Justice in Morocco. Regarding chains of outcomes, DIHR's research agenda and partnerships with Governmental Human Rights Focal Points (GHRFPs) in the MENA region and West Africa, have contributed to shaping the global agenda, discussions, and processes on National Mechanisms for Implementation, Reporting and Follow-up (NMIRF). The initiative by the states of Morocco, Paraguay and Portugal to establish a global NMIRF network - a commitment made at the DIHR-supported Marrakesh seminar in 2022 - is a concrete example of how DIHR expertise has fed into global NMIRF processes. Moreover, 'In May 2023, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Paraguay confirmed that they would organise a follow-up seminar to the Marrakech Declaration, with the seminar taking placing in May 2024 in Asuncion', Outcome ID: DI02210. The need and relevance for the establishment of a network between NMIRFs have been advocated and recommended for many years by the DIHR, the Human Rights Council and the OHCHR. Several reports and Human Rights Council Resolutions have been adopted including the recent Human Right Council Resolution number 51/33 on NMIRF promoted by Paraguay. In late 2023, DIHR published a research study on interactions between NHRIs and NMIRFs , which critically explores their roles and complementarity and proposes recommendations on how they can engage constructively while respecting their distinct roles and mandates. This study uses Denmark as one of its case-studies and serves as a basis for discussion and programming with potential and new partners. The outcome stated above is rated 'important'following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.

title.narrative: 4.2 We have captured change and adapted through learning, context and research knowledge and partnerships.

DIHR has at least 4 regional offices that are firmly rooted through context knowledge and functions as coordinating entities between DIHR HQ and partners and stakeholders. All new initiatives have been subject to context analysis.

target.value: All new initiatives initiated in 2023 have developed or updated context analysis and theories of change. All regional local offices are key liaison and implementation entities between DIHR HQ and local stakeholders. New initiatives are increasingly initiated from DIHR's regional local offices. A stock-taking exercise about the role and efficiency of the regional local offices set up vis-a-vis HQ has been undertaken.

actual.value: 1. New initiatives have developed or updated context analysis and theories of change as per their project documents. 2 to 4 Regarding regional local offices, in 2023, as part of the stock-taking exercise, it was decided that the most effective way of improving the co-ordination of partnerships and activities as well as the outreach of DIHR in specific countries was to shift the emphasis from establishing regional offices to establishing or consolidating country offices which have greater proximity and easy access to partners, project activities and potential donors. In this way, DIHR also managed to counter the risk of creating an extra organisational layer . It is, however, important to notice that all country offices are expected to have a strong regional outlook and engagement. Thus, offices exist in Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Jordan, Mali, Niger, Tunisia, Zambia and Colombia. Our office in Colombia retains the nomination 'regional office' since it drives implementation of activities and outreach throughout Latin America. The offices in Burkina Faso, Jordan Ethiopia, Mali, Niger and Tunisia are DED co-funded. DIHR also took steps to start up an office in Uganda, but by end of 2023 the status on this indicator adds up to 7 offices with DED funding. These local offices are playing a key role in undertaking new initiatives as well as during the implementation phase including the liaison with local stakeholders.

actual.value: The initiatives counted under this indicator include: the Responsible Business Conduct (RBC) agreement for renewable energy, the NHRI group under the EU due diligence project (co-funded by DED); the EU legal instruments regulating human rights in global values chains (numerous including the CSDDD); the OECD (Revised its Guidelines for Multinational Entreprises); Finance in Common Working Group on Human Rights as well as Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) Advance. Regarding chains of changes, an example outcome is: 'In May 2024, three companies of the Responsible Business Conduct (RBC) Agreement on Renewable Energy launched a collective action project. The project will allow small-scale miners from Southern Peru to participate in formal supply chains based on a due diligence framework tailored to their needs and challenges'. This is rather significant since 100.000 people are dedicated to small scale copper mining in Peru. Many are women and the majority are Indigenous, Quechua -speaking people. The collaborative approach, knowledge production, outreach, and advocacy will foster the integration of such small-scale miners into responsible supply chains of transition minerals worldwide. It will also set precedent for direct and efficient engagement of energy companies on their mineral supply chain. This is the first time that renewable energy companies will engage directly with the most vulnerable suppliers to help address their sustainability challenges, rather than exclude them. DIHR connected the RBC Agreement with the local NGO that leads the project and co-developed the project proposal. As part of the project implementation, DIHR is ensuring that HRBA is applied in all processes and products. DIHR also supports the development of a grievance mechanism for the sector. Thus, this outcome is outcome is rated 'important' following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.

title.narrative: 2.2 Support a human rights-based implementation of the 2030 Agenda that ensures no one is left behind

4 global, and regional sustainable development and human rights actors are using human rights tools and data to accelerate Sustainable Development Goals implementation and ensure accountability for groups of rightsholders

target.value: At least two additional partnerships are recorded regarding integrated implementation of human rights and Sustainable Development Goals. For each partner, at least one chain of changes is recorded regarding integrated implementation and monitoring of human rights and Sustainable Development Goals.

actual.value: DIHR formalized the partnership with the Working Group on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR): Conducted a joint panel session with the ACHPR and NANHRI focusing on using the 2030 Agenda as leverage for promoting human rights change in the region. Agreed to conduct joint study in 2023 DIHR also firmed up collaboration with the UN Statistical Division (UNSD): Contributed as panellists in the UN Inter Agency Expert Group on SDG Data Agreed to collaborate around events at the 2023 World Data Forum Initiated dialogue on a joint project proposal for the World Bank Human Rights Trust Fund on data partnerships.

target.value: At least one additional partnership is recorded regarding integrated implementation of human rights and Sustainable Development Goals. Previous chains of changes are continued and at least one chain of change is recorded with significance valued no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per partner

actual.value: DIHR has prioritised collaboration with 4 regional and global actors funded by the DED, namely the Working Group on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) regarding a study on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ESCR) and national development plans, partly the using the DIHR Human Rights Algorithm, the UN Statistical Division (UNSD) on using citizen-generated data as well as the Asia Pacific Forum of NHRIs (APF), and the UN Economic and Social Commission in Latin America (ECLAC) on using the 'Rights to Defend Rights' tool. An example of a outcome from this type of chain of changes is 'In February 2023, the UN Statistical Commission, which is the highest governance body for the work of National Statistical Offices (NSOs), requested the UN Statistics Division (UNSD) to develop a conceptual framework for citizen-generated data, and supported the establishment of a collaborative on citizen data to inform the development of guidance to NSOs and citizens working on this'. This is important since frameworks endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission are acknowledged by National Statistical Offices, and thus likely to influence their work. Having a framework and guidance on citizen data is a crucial step towards getting National Statistical Offices on board for national level cooperation with rights-holder-driven data collection initiatives. DIHR and partners have been advocating the UN Statistical Division to place emphasis on the data generated by citizens, including support to our work with the 'Indigenous Navigator'and the 'Right to Defend Rights' tools. Thus, in 2023, DIHR hosted an Expert Group Meeting on citizen data, leading to the 'Copenhagen Framework on Citizen Data', which is a contribution to development of new global norms on citizen data. The above-mentioned outcome is rated 'important' following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.

target.value: At least one additional partnership is recorded regarding integrated implementation and monitoring of human rights and Sustainable Development Goals

actual.value: Results achieved

target.value: Chains of changes are continued. ACHPR has used DIHRs algorithm to facilitate the analysis of 52 national development plans in Africa (cf. outcome DI02853). Regarding the UN Statistical Commission, we have worked with them for several years on citizen data (cf. outcome DI02721). In relation to the Asia Pacific Forum, they have been engaged in the Rights to Defend Rights Tool and in 2024 the APF decided to roll out the tool in the Asia-Pacific region. The Institute developed a training module for APFs elearning course on human rights defenders for NHRIs in the region and provided technical support on the use of indicators and data to monitor the enabling environment for human rights defenders. In Latin America, the dialogue with ECLAC on exploring the use of the Rights to Defend Rights Tool in the context of monitoring the Escazu Agreements provisions on environmental defenders continued in 2024, but still with no tangible results

actual.value: The four countries under the first indicator regarding state actors are Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda, and Colombia. In Tanzania, the NHRI, as part of the Steering Committee and Technical Committee for the National Action Plan (NAP) on Business and Human Rights, developed thematic working groups, timelines, budgets, and strategies for resource mobilization related to the NAP. An advanced draft of the NAP is now awaiting submission to the relevant government Ministry, followed by national validation. In Ethiopia, the NHRI strengthened the capacity of its staff to monitor the impacts of business projects on human rights, while also engaging in NAPrelated advocacy with other stakeholders, particularly the Multistakeholder Forum on Business and Human Rights. In Uganda during 2024, organizers of the Uganda-EU business forum hosted a session on responsible business that DIHR co-designed, and in which the NHRI was involved. The NHRI also provided substantive input to the Sixth Annual Symposium on Business and Human Rights, which was co-organized by the Ministry for Gender, Labour and Social Development (MGLSD), the responsible entity for the NAP. In Colombia, because of the engagement with the Environmental Agency, the Agency has requested training on human rights from the Institute and has incorporated some human rights concepts in the draft Guidance for the Elaboration of Environmental Impact Assessments published for consultation and have committed to further work on these topics.

target.value: The chain(s) of changes recorded in year one is continued in year 2; for each partner, at least one new chain of change is recorded re development / adoption / implementation of National Action Plans and/or other measures to address business and human rights challenges.

actual.value:
Undertook strengthening partnerships with African NHRIs attending 2022 Africa BHR Forum, and a peer learning initiative on BHR.
Training Addis Ababa University Center for HR that in 2022 carried out investigation regarding floriculture industry. Collaboration Ethiopian Women in Energy network.
Deepened collaboration with Uganda Human Rights Commission and Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development on BHR.

target.value: Chains of changes are continued. For each partner, at least one chain of change is recorded by peer assessor with significance valued no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per partner.

actual.value: Until now, three countries are included under this indicator which are Tanzania, Uganda and Ethiopia. In Uganda the NHRI has piloted a new tool for monitoring of business activities and the Ministry of Gender and Social Affairs capacitated local authorities on the National Action Plan (NAP) on Business and Human Rights. In Tanzania the NHRI engaged in monitoring of Business and Human Rights and has set up a Steering Committee for the NAP. In Ethiopia a multistakeholder alliance for Business and Human Rights has been established by the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC). In addition, through the innovation fund, in 2023 a scoping for a sectoral human rights impact assessment of wind energy in Colombia was conducted. An example of an outcome from a chain of changes in Tanzania is: 'On 5-6 December 2023, the National Action Plan Steering Committee convened for the first time in Arusha, Tanzania and agreed on the way forward and a roadmap for the development of the National Action Plan (NAP) on Business and Human Rights'. The National Action Plan Steering Committee is leading the development of the NAP and the NAP Roadmap enabled that the process is moving forward. There are 7 thematic working groups already established by the committee comprising government and CSOs representatives to assist it in carrying out research and stakeholder consultations toward the development of the Tanzania NAP. The thematic groups are established in sectors: Extractives and Energy; Manufacturing and Processing; Agriculture and Blue Economy; Tourism and Hospitality; Works and Transportation; Trade and Finance; Telecommunication and Digital Economy. The NAP process was supported through technical assistance to the Commission for Human Rights and Good Governance (CHRAGG) in the development of the NAP Roadmap. This was requested by the Tanzanian Government, and it assigned CHRAGG a lead role in coordinating the process. DIHR and CHRAGG collaborated to host a workshop for the newly appointed NAP Steering Committee, where participants jointly developed terms of reference for their roles and responsibilities and sketched the way forward for the consultations, research and engagement needed for the NAP. This outcome has been rated 'moderate'following the the Outcome Harvesting definitions, but it is expected that 'important' outcomes will be produced in this chain of changes during 2024.

title.narrative: 1.2 Support rule of law by well-functioning national and regional human rights systems

The DED has supported, including through co-financing of EU financed projects, strengthening the capacity of 13 security actors in Africa to become human rights compliant, underpinned by strategic collaboration with the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights.

target.value: Chains of changes from 2022 are continued. At least one chain of change is recorded with significance valued no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per partner.

actual.value: As per end of 2023, 13 security actors have been supported with co-funding from the DED. In Burkina Faso this includes 4 security actors: Police National, Corps des eaux et forets, Gendarmerie, Garde de securite penitentiaire (all until January 2024). In Mali DIHR has also supported 4 security actors: Police National (until January 2024), Garde National, Gendarmerie, Garde de securite penitentaiare (until January 2023). And in Niger 3 security actors: Police National, Garde National, Gendarmerie (all until July 2023). On the regional level in Sahel, DIHR has worked with the police network, POLI-DH (until July 2023). And finally, DIHR has recently started working with the Uganda Prisons Service, fully funded by the DED. Regarding chains of outcomes, an example of an outcome in this area is: 'During 2023, in Mali, the general conditions of detention in the prisons, police stations and gendarmerie brigades monitored by the National Commission on Human Rights have become more humane', Outcome ID: DI02572. This means that acts of torture as well as degrading and inhumane practices are gradually disappearing from the monitored prisons, police stations and gendarmerie brigades in addition to significant improvements in keeping records on detainees and prisoners. The contribution of DIHR is the elaboration and establishment of tools and training on human rights as part of security actor training curriculum as well as the support to the National Commission on Human Rights. This entails a chain of changes of which the outcome stated above is rated as of 'major' significance following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.

title.narrative: 1.3 Support rule of law by well-functioning national and regional human rights systems
4 state or non-state justice actors in minimum 2 countries in Africa are equipped to provide effective justice services, which are available, accessible, acceptable, and of good quality.

target.value: Chains of changes from 2022 are continued. At least one chain of change in each country is recorded with significance valued no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per partner

actual.value: In the work with state or non-state justice actors, the DED funded work has focussed on the latter with 2 CSOs in Kenya, namely Citizen Participation Forum (CIPAF) and Ripples International, and 1 university legal clinic in Uganda namely Public Interest Law Clinic (PILAC). Regarding chains of changes, outcomes from Kenya include: 'On diverse dates from 1 July 2023 to 31 December 2023, 27 Legal Literacy Volunteers from 14 Community Reconciliation Centres in Meru County successfully settled 426 legal disputes through mediation. This is the first time that this number of disputes relating to family matters have been settled without having to go through the formal court process'. It is important that community members within areas where Community Reconciliation Centres are located were able to access legal information and assistance from the Legal Literacy Volunteers in order to seek justice. By resolving cases within the community through mediation, those seeking justice avoid costly and delayed court processes which are often inaccessible to them. In addition, the increase in cases being resolved out of court reduces the Meru Law Courts' caseload. It also demonstrates that communities are building trust in the Legal Literacy Volunteers to provide assistance to them in resolving disputes within the community, promoting a reconciliatory approach to dispute resolution which helps to promote community cohesiveness. The contribution of DIHR was to train the Legal Literacy Volunteers on human rights issues, focussing on women's rights and sexual and gender-based violence. DIHR also initiated the development of a manual for the Legal Literacy Volunteers. In addition, DIHR has worked closely with the CSO partner, Ripples, to ensure the establishment of the Community Reconciliation Centres. These chains of changes have led to the above-mentioned outcome which is rated 'important' following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.

target.value: The chain(s) of changes recorded in year 2021 is continued in 2022; at least one new chain of change in each partner country regarding the provision of effective justice services, which are which are which are available, accessible, acceptable, and of good quality.

actual.value: Partnerships with two CSOs in Kenya were initiated to enhance access to justice for rights-holders in poor and marginalised communities in Baringo and Meru counties through strengthening alternative justice systems and ensuring that justice delivered complies with human rights and constitutional standards.

In Meru County, the Institute cooperated with the CSO Ripples International to influence similar AJS local authorities. This went together with influencing actors at national level such as the Anti-Female Genital Mutilation Board and the National Steering Committee on the Implementation of the Alternative Justice System Policy in Kenya. In Uganda, the access to justice work included a university legal clinic in Uganda namely Public Interest Law Clinic (PILAC) as well as UPS Finally, in Ethiopia, DIHR started a pilot initiative with the MoJ regarding technical and financial support for the MoJs monitoring mandate to visit correctional facilities and police stations to monitor the treatment of detainees and conditions of detention. Thus, the actors counted in the indicator are the CSOs CIPAF, Ripples and PILAC as well as state actors comprising of the UPS in Uganda and on youth and / or other rights holders the MoJ in Ethiopia.

actual.value: For the engagement on youth and/or other rights holders, there has been a DED-funded engagement with the Palestinian Independent Commission for Human Rights (ICHR) on supporting student-led initiatives on human rights. Secondly, a partnership has been entered into with the Youth Movement for Development and the Civic Education (MOJEDEC), which is a youth based CSO in Niger. Thirdly, DIHR has worked with youth from various civil society organizations in Jordan to engage in the UPR process. Moreover, in Kenya, there are many outcomes involving rights holders and human rights actors at provincial and local level. One example is: 'Between November 2022 and October 2023, all police stations within Baringo Central, Baringo North, Baringo South and Tiaty sub-counties in Kenya allocated separate rooms for alternative dispute resolution and mediation related activities'. This is important since allocating separate rooms within the police stations for alternative dispute resolution, including mediation, provides parties with a conducive environment to discuss and find amicable solutions to their problem. It also leads to less conflict in the community, and it promotes reconciliation instead of prolonged court cases, thereby reducing court backlogs and congestion in prisons. In order to achieve this, DIHR and the partner CIPAF did a training on Alternative Justice Systems for police officers (Security Sector Actor) in September 2022. The discussions from the training are what influenced the idea for separate room for alternative dispute resolution and mediation initiatives at the police stations. This outcome is part of a chain of changes regarding the county-level Justice System and is rated 'important' following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.

title.narrative: 2.1 Support a human rights-based implementation of the 2030 Agenda that ensures no one is left behind
State actors in 4 countries have capacity and tools to ensure integrated implementation of human right and Sustainable Development Goals with accountability for rightsholders

target.value: At least two additional partnerships are recorded regarding integrated implementation of human rights and Sustainable Development Goals. Previous chains of changes are continued, and in each partner country at least one chain of change is valued no lower than 'important' by peer assessor per partner.

actual.value: DIHR has prioritised partnerships with actors in 3 priority countries, namely Kenya, Honduras and Colombia. In Kenya DIHR has partnered with the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights throughout the DED implementation period, with a focus on a rights-based approach to data, generation of human rights data on different themes, and data-driven promotion of human rights. In Honduras, DIHR has established collaboration with the NHRI CONADEH on human rights education in primary and secondary schools and collaborated with other organisations on the situation of human rights defenders. In Colombia, DIHR has worked with the NHRI on human rights education, and also established a partnership with the Colombian Commission of Jurists, to assess the enabling space for human rights defenders. Regarding chains of changes, the following outcome is part of a chain of changes on sustainable development in Kenya: 'In September 2023, in Kenya, the Social Protection Secretariat, Ministry of Labour and Social Protection incorporated the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) into the technical working group currently developing the National Social Protection Bill'. This is significant as it will enable KNCHR to directly influence the Social Protection Bill from a human rights perspective. DIHR has contributed by supporting KNCHR to document human rights gaps in the implementation of the right to social security and has supported KNCHR with peer learning, mentoring and guidance as well as financial support to systematically monitor the right. KNCHR has been in the driving seat with support and backstopping from DIHR. This outcome is rated 'important' following the Outcome Harvesting definitions.
